reason: The sources support a highly dramatic 45-second story with 16 distinct, cross-referenced claims from multiple independent websites regarding this near-miss catastrophe.
story: On July 23, 2012, the Sun launched an ultra-fast solar superstorm that tore through Earth's orbit. It was a Carrington-class coronal mass ejection, packing the power of a billion hydrogen bombs and traveling four times faster than normal. Had it hit, the consequences would have been catastrophic, inflicting over two trillion dollars in damage and knocking out power grids and water supplies globally. Experts estimate recovery would have taken up to ten years. Yet, the public barely noticed. Why? Because the storm missed Earth by a margin of just nine days. Instead of wiping out our modern power grid, the blast hit NASA’s STEREO-A spacecraft, which was safely positioned outside Earth's magnetosphere to record the event. The storm's path had been cleared by a smaller solar eruption four days earlier, allowing it to maintain its terrifying speed. Scientists warn there is a twelve percent chance a similar Carrington-class storm will strike Earth in any given decade.
angle: An ultra-powerful solar storm matching the 1859 Carrington Event missed Earth by just nine days in July 2012, which would have knocked out our power grids and water supplies for up to a decade.

claims.claim: On July 23, 2012, a major solar storm involving an exceptionally powerful coronal mass ejection occurred.
The storm missed Earth by a margin of only about nine days because the erupting region of the Sun was no longer pointed directly at us.
The July 2012 eruption was comparable in strength to the historic 1859 Carrington Event.
Had the storm hit Earth, it would have caused catastrophic damage to global power grids, satellite communications, and electronic systems.
A direct hit from the storm could have caused global economic damages exceeding 2 trillion dollars.
The recovery time for humanity to bounce back from such a solar disaster was estimated to be between 4 and 10 years.
Widespread water and plumbing supplies would have been knocked out because urban pumps rely on electricity.
Instead of hitting Earth, the massive plasma blast struck NASA's STEREO-A solar observatory spacecraft.
The STEREO-A spacecraft survived the blast because it was in interplanetary space, outside Earth's magnetosphere where strong, damaging induced electrical currents do not form.
The 1859 Carrington Event was so intense that it knocked out telegraph networks, shocked operators, and caused telegraph lines to spark and catch fire.
During the 1859 Carrington Event, the auroras were visible incredibly far south, including Cuba and Hawaii.
A smaller solar storm in March 1989 knocked out the power grid in Quebec, Canada, leaving millions of people without electricity.
The peak speed of the 2012 storm's magnetic cloud exceeded 2,000 kilometers per second, which is about four times faster than a typical solar storm.
The extreme speed of the 2012 storm was achieved because another CME four days earlier had cleared the path of material that would normally slow it down.
The 2012 event actually consisted of at least two nearly simultaneous coronal mass ejections separated by only 10 to 15 minutes.
Physicist Pete Riley calculated there is a 12% probability of a Carrington-class solar storm striking Earth within any given ten-year period.

disputed: The exact margin of the near-miss: S1, S6, and S7 state the storm missed Earth by 'roughly nine days', while S2, S4, and S5 state 'one week' or 'a week'. The script should resolve this by stating 'about a week to nine days' or 'nine days'.

The peak speed of the CME: S1 notes a radial speed of 3,300 km/s and an average speed of 2,000 km/s; S3 and S6 cite a peak speed of more than 2,000 km/s; S5 cites 3,000 km/s, and S7 cites 2,500-3,000 km/s. The script should generalise this by saying 'over 2,000 kilometers per second' or 'four times faster than normal'.
Where the 1859 aurora was visible: S2 and S5 mention Cuba, while S3 and S6 mention Hawaii. The script can attribute this widely by saying 'seen in tropical latitudes like Cuba and Hawaii'.
